one_line_contribution: A pre-registered measurement claiming an upper bound on query-agnostic memory curation: with a frozen bank and injection volume held exactly fixed, the best static policy attainable — LOO-best constant configuration, set-level oracle prune, GEPA search, sequential bank editor — sits within ~2-3 points of random equal-volume selection, while an untrained query-conditional cross-encoder reranker at identical k does not, with a matched-volume random-removal control that separates published curation gains from bank shrinkage.
closest_prior_work: Two threats, and the proposal only fully absorbs one. (a) arXiv:2603.02473 ("Diagnosing Retrieval vs. Utilization Bottlenecks in LLM Agent Memory") already establishes the direction on a 3x3 write x retrieve factorial; the proposal concedes this and re-centres on the bound, the volume control, and the variance decomposition, which is the right move. (b) The larger and unabsorbed threat is classical query-conditional demonstration selection — KATE (Liu et al. 2021) and Rubin et al. (2022) — combined with datamodel/DemoShapley-style attribution showing near-null marginal per-example effects. Once you accept both, "a constant policy cannot exploit item x query interaction, a retrieval-conditioned one can" is close to analytic rather than empirical. The proposal cites KATE/Rubin and argues the new content is the oracle-strength static side and the zero-supervision conditional side, but that framing only survives if the static arms are genuinely as strong as claimed — see the objection below, where they are not.
strongest_objection: The design does not measure the class it names, and the two arms carrying the headline are both weaker than advertised. (1) Every 'query-agnostic' arm still runs the BGE retriever at read time: C1/C3/C4/C9/C10 prune the bank and then retrieve top-4, and P0/P1/P2/P3 range over rank patterns defined on the retriever's own top-12. So P1 is not 'the ceiling on any query-agnostic policy' — it is the ceiling over 8 size-4 rank patterns drawn from a single retriever's top-12, a pool engineered to be near-homogeneous. F1 (P1-P0 <= 2) is therefore close to a foregone conclusion and, whatever its CI, it does not license the title's claim about write-time curation. Correspondingly, C6-vs-C3 is not 'conditional beats static at matched information' but 'read-time reranking of top-12 beats bank pruning followed by top-4 retrieval' — a comparison of decision-time information, not of policy class. (2) The C3 'set-level oracle static prune fitted on unlimited probe data' is, by the proposal's own numbers, fitted on ~70 binary observations per item with a stated per-item detectable effect of +-22 points, on a target (the marginal item main effect) that the paper's own thesis predicts is ~0 and that F8 predicts almost no item will clear. An estimator with +-22-point per-item resolution is not an oracle, and the sentence 'a null here cannot be blamed on a weak estimator' is exactly what a reviewer will contest. The claim that the bound is a property of the class 'and not of estimator quality, search budget, or training signal' rests entirely on C3, and C3 cannot bear it. (3) The bank is 400 trajectories distilled by a frontier model and deduped to 120 items — i.e. already curated before the audit begins. Nulls across C1/C3/C9/C10 are then uninterpretable: they are consistent with 'no query-agnostic policy can work' and equally with 'this particular bank has almost no removable harm', and nothing in the design distinguishes them. (4) Power on the headline is razor-thin by the proposal's own arithmetic: F2 predicts P2-P1 >= 5 against an MDE of 4.4, while P2 must learn query-feature interactions from only 199 training queries with a 32-dim query PCA plus per-rank features — branch C is not a tail risk, it is the modal outcome.
what_would_fix_it: Four changes, in priority order. (1) A positive control with a spiked bank: inject a known set of harmful/contradictory items and verify that C1, C3, C9 and C10 actually remove them and that removal recovers performance. Without a demonstrated detection floor, the whole audit's null is unfalsifiable. (2) Make C3 a real oracle: fit the set-level prune transductively on the Phase-3 instances themselves (in-sample within-pool ceiling), or raise Phase-2 coverage until per-item resolution is comparable to the +-3-point null band. A ceiling claim needs an oracle that is powered on the quantity it optimizes. (3) Widen P1's hypothesis class beyond retriever rank patterns to include content-defined static packages selected independently of the retriever's per-query ordering, so 'query-agnostic' is not smuggling a query-conditional component; and report P1 with the retriever ablated (fixed random top-12 pool) as the true static reference. (4) Add the composition arm — curated bank (C1 or C3) plus the C6 reranker — since the actionable claim ('write-time curation is bounded, spend the budget at read time') requires showing curation adds nothing on top of a good read-time policy, not merely that it loses to one. Also vary bank size/noise (e.g. 120 vs 500 items, deduped vs raw) so the ceiling is reported as a function of bank quality rather than measured once on the most favourable bank for the hypothesis. Separately, the compute arithmetic is wrong by roughly an order of magnitude: at the stated 3,000 tok/s aggregate and ~7,200 generated tokens/episode (8 calls x 900), throughput is ~0.4 episodes/s, not 3, giving ~1,500 episodes/hour before the 3x tool-latency discount and ~500/hour after — 26,200 episodes is ~50 GPU-hours of generation alone, before ~2.5B tokens of prefill, so '7 GPU-hours' and 'under 3 days including a full re-run' should be restated as 1-2 weeks of node time.
missing_baseline: Two. (a) A positive control / spiked-bank sanity arm establishing that the curation conditions can detect item-level harm at all — its absence makes every static null ambiguous between 'the policy class is bounded' and 'this bank had nothing to prune'. (b) A composition arm: static curation AND read-time conditional selection together (C1+C6, C3+C6) against C6 alone. The paper's recommendation — write-time curation is not worth the budget, fill the demonstration slot at read time — is a claim about complementarity that the plan never tests; write-time and read-time selection are not mutually exclusive in any deployed system. Third, minor but a reviewer will ask: an oracle read-time selector at k=4 over the full 495 size-4 subsets, to show how much of the conditional headroom the 8-pattern pool is hiding on the conditional side too.
preprint_collision: The check is unusually strong for this genre and should be credited: it names a directional collision (arXiv:2603.02473) rather than hiding it, retracts a prior unverifiable MEMAUDIT anchor, admits it could retrieve only title/venue for the audited target A-MAC (arXiv:2603.04549), reports three search passes, and states the residual risk (a matched-volume random-removal ablation buried in a recent curation appendix) explicitly. I find no preprint that makes the specific bound claim. But two gaps remain. First, the check searches the agent-memory literature and not the adjacent context-compression / selective-RAG literature, where random-drop and random-sentence-removal controls at matched token budget are routine; the claim that matched-volume random removal is 'absent from every curation paper we found' is true only under a narrow reading of 'curation paper', and a reviewer from the compression side will say the control is standard practice being rebranded as a contribution. Second, the check does not search for prior oracle-static-vs-conditional demonstration-selection comparisons in the ICL literature, which is where the proposal's own Related Work section (4) concedes the direction was anticipated by KATE and Rubin et al.; a novelty claim resting on 'the static side is an oracle this time' should have been searched for directly, and was not. Net: the collision check is honest and current, and it correctly reduces the claimed novelty of direction, but it leaves the two searches that most threaten what remains.
